title: Defence entrepreneurs dispel gold-rush mentality amid federal spending boom
html:
Minister of National Defence David McGuinty is shown a Rheinmetall Mission Master SP, an electric unmanned ground vehicle made in Canada, during GCXpo 2026, a demonstration showcase of Canadian next-gen tech, at Area X.O in Ottawa, on Sept. 29.Justin Tang/The Canadian Press

Canadian defence entrepreneurs say they are struggling under the weight of short-term contracts, a lack of funding and a distaste for risk within the federal government despite the messaging from Ottawa about the windfall of opportunity for their industry.

Ravi Ramsaran, chief executive officer of artificial-intelligence company Nextria Inc., said that as a software provider, he often has to counter the perception that a firehose of funds is flowing into Canadian defence and automatically creating a bigger market.

“That’s been one of the challenges – trying to dispel this myth that there’s this huge cache of money that’s just sitting here and we’re taking it, when it’s really not like that,” he said during a panel discussion at a defence robotics conference in Ottawa last week.

The conference brought together industry, military and government on the grounds of Area X.O, a research and development facility not far from the Ottawa airport, to demonstrate and discuss the opportunity for defence robotics in Canada.

In an hour-long address, General Wayne Eyre, former chief of the defence staff, set the tone for the current moment.

“We’re living through a period in which the assumptions that shaped Canada for so many decades, for Canadian security, Canada’s place in the world, they are rapidly changing, and in many cases being overturned,” he told the crowd.

Robotics are central to how militaries operate, Gen. Eyre said, and the entrepreneurs building these technologies need consistent feedback to develop and improve their products and meet the requirements of the Canadian Armed Forces.

“This is an adaptation battle, and that rapid, collaborative feedback is absolutely essential,” he said.

But Mr. Ramsaran hasn’t been able to find that consistency in Canada, after years of trying. Traditionally, about 95 per cent of his customer base has been in this country. Today, that’s changing out of necessity, as Mr. Ramsaran said he’s looking elsewhere for work that doesn’t come in spurts, or short-term contracts affiliated with military operations, like it does at home.

“As an AI company, that’s the death knell for me because AI isn’t just about ‘Here’s a capability,’ leave it on the floor and then leave. It’s not a piece of equipment,” he said.

“It’s really about getting a long-term relationship with the CAF so that we both are learning together, and that does not exist.”

The Department of National Defence did not respond to The Globe and Mail’s request for comment about challenges being faced by industry.

Michael Nelson, chief executive at Tactiql Inc., said his company also encounters difficulties as a software provider working in defence – but for different reasons.

Over the summer, the veteran said, his company was closing in on a contract with the Canadian Armed Forces for its technology, which normalizes data from various sensors into ingestible information for systems that support decision-making. However, despite funding being previously secured, Mr. Nelson said he found out his contract was on the chopping block as a result of budget cuts.

“That was the first warning sign in a daisy chain of events,” he said during the panel discussion.

What Mr. Nelson later learned is that the Department of National Defence uses the same bucket of funding – Vote 1, or operating expenditures – to buy software like his and to pay for operations and maintenance, as well as programs such as the Cadets. Capital expenditures, such as major equipment procurements, fall into a separate bucket called Vote 5.

As Ottawa reprioritized funds for certain purchases and to meet its defence spending targets, as agreed upon by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Mr. Nelson said he was told funding was reallocated from Vote 1 to Vote 5, and that’s why his contract suddenly fell through.

The federal government’s supplementary estimates for this fiscal year and the previous one illustrate internal transfers from Vote 1 into Vote 5 for several initiatives, including the Canadian Coast Guard’s maritime security mandate and Ottawa’s Capital Investment Fund. Most of the department’s transfers of funds to other government branches also came out of Vote 1 both years, though Vote 1 was on the receiving end for some transfers into defence for specific projects.

Programs such as the country’s Cadets, whose operations also fall under Vote 1, have been affected by curtailed spending, too, as they were recently ordered to suspend certain activities. (Ottawa ultimately backpedalled on this decision owing to public outcry.)

“For those of us that are reliant on Vote 1 funding, including the reserves, including the Cadets, including lots of us, we’re in a big struggle right now,” Mr. Nelson said.

That’s not to say that energy and excitement aren’t present in the sector. Mr. Ramsaran said the past six years are “the best that it’s ever been, from a Canadian perspective.”

But the momentum must keep going if selling into defence in Canada is going to get any easier or faster. Case in point: Mr. Ramsaran said he has multiple deals close to completion right now.

But, he added, they’ve been that way for about seven months and will likely take a couple more before they’re completed. “That’s the reality of being a defence company.”
summary: Some software companies say they encounter difficulties with short-term contracts, lack of funding
